opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's one of the most exciting directions right now. The way we've been doing things for a while, especially with reinforcement learning for legged robots, is that you train one policy for walking on rough terrain, another one for climbing stairs, maybe another for jumping or getting up after a fall. Each of them works pretty well in its own domain, but then you need some kind of high-level switching logic to decide which one to run, and the transitions between them are often where things break. You end up with a fragile system that's only as good as the handcrafted glue between the pieces.

If you merge those skills into a single model, a few good things happen. First, the transitions become part of what the policy learns, so instead of an abrupt switch from "walking mode" to "climbing mode," the robot can blend smoothly between behaviors based on what it's actually perceiving. Second, you get transfer between skills. A lot of the underlying knowledge is shared: balance, understanding contact, estimating terrain from sensors. When one network learns all of that together, the representations tend to be richer and more robust than when each skill learns them in isolation. We've seen cases where training on a broader set of tasks actually makes the policy better at each individual task, because it's seen more variety.

And third, and maybe most importantly in the long term, it moves us toward something that looks more like a foundation model for robotics. Once you have one general model, you can condition it on different commands or goals, fine-tune it for new tasks with much less data, and start to see emergent behaviors you didn't explicitly design. That's very hard to get when you have a zoo of specialized controllers.

Of course, it's not free. Bigger, multi-task models are harder to train, you can get interference between tasks, and you need to be careful that the model still runs fast enough on the robot's onboard compute. Approaches like distillation help a lot there. You can train specialized expert policies in simulation, which is relatively easy, and then distill them into one student policy that captures all of them. That's been a really practical way to get the best of both worlds.

r001.rationale: It says a single policy can “blend smoothly between behaviors” instead of switching abruptly, expressing interpolation between skills.

r002.rationale: It describes distilling specialized simulation-trained expert policies into one student, but does not propose a unified vision-language-action model trained on simulation data generated by those separate models.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we've been thinking about a lot. Right now, the way most of us in legged robotics work is that you train one policy for one task. You have a policy for walking over rough terrain, you have another one for parkour, maybe a separate one for getting up after a fall, another for opening a door. Each of these is trained in simulation, often with its own reward design, its own curriculum, its own set of tricks. And they work really well individually. But then when you want to deploy on the real robot, you end up with this patchwork of controllers and some kind of hand-designed state machine switching between them. That's fragile, and more importantly, it doesn't scale.

So the first and most obvious benefit of merging them is just engineering simplicity. One model, one interface, you don't have to worry about transitions between skills, because the transitions become part of what the model learns. A lot of the failures we see on hardware actually happen exactly at those boundaries, when you hand over from one controller to another and the state the robot is in doesn't quite match what the next policy expects.

But I think the more interesting argument is about generalization. When you train skills separately, each policy only ever sees its own narrow distribution of situations. If you combine them, the model is forced to share representations. The walking skill and the climbing skill both have to understand something about contact, about where the robot's feet are relative to the terrain, about momentum. If those are learned jointly, you tend to get a more robust understanding of the robot's dynamics, and you start to see behaviors emerge in situations that were never explicitly in any of the individual training sets. The robot might combine a bit of what it learned for stepping over obstacles with what it learned for recovering from a push, and handle a scenario that neither skill alone would have handled.

Now, I want to be honest that it's not free. There's a real tension. Specialist policies are usually better at their specific task than a generalist, at least initially. When you merge them, you often lose a bit of peak performance on each skill, and you have to deal with issues like gradient interference, where improving one skill hurts another. Scaling up the network helps, better architectures help, and one approach we've found promising is to use the specialist policies as teachers. You train the experts first, where it's easy to get really strong performance, and then distill them into a single student policy. That way you don't have to solve the hard multi-task exploration problem from scratch, you just have to compress knowledge that already exists.

And the longer-term thing I find exciting is that once you have a single model with a broad repertoire, you have something you can condition on higher-level commands. Whether that's a language instruction or an output from some planner, the lower-level model knows how to execute. That's really the direction I think the field is going. We're moving from asking "can the robot do this one impressive thing" to "can the robot do whatever we ask it to," and you can't get there with a hundred separate policies.

r001.rationale: The response describes the merged model combining aspects of skills such as obstacle stepping and push recovery to handle situations neither skill handled alone, expressing the hoped-for interpolation between skills.

r002.rationale: It proposes distilling specialist policies into a student, but does not propose a unified vision-language-action model trained on simulation data generated by those specialists.

astra-6.text:
I think the exciting possibility is that the skills can start to help each other. If you train locomotion separately from manipulation, you have a robot that knows how to walk and a robot that knows how to move an object, but combining those two behaviors is still a challenge. A single model could potentially coordinate them—adjusting its stance while reaching, for example, or moving its body to make a manipulation task easier.

And you would hope that sharing what it learns across tasks makes learning new skills more efficient. Instead of starting from scratch every time, the model already has some useful understanding of how its body interacts with the environment.

But simply putting the skills into one model doesn’t guarantee that you get that transfer. It might just reproduce the separate behaviors, or even get worse at some of them. The interesting question is whether it can combine those skills in situations it wasn’t explicitly trained for. That’s where you’d really start to see the benefit of a more general model.

r001.rationale: The response hopes the model will coordinate and combine skills in new situations, but it does not identify interpolation between skills as a capability.

r002.rationale: It does not propose a unified vision-language-action model or training it on simulation data generated by separate skill models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the exciting part is that these skills could start to help each other. If you train a model just for locomotion, it learns how to move the robot around. If you train another model for manipulation, it learns how to interact with objects. But a lot of useful tasks require both—you need to move into position, maintain your balance, and manipulate something at the same time.

If we can bring those capabilities into one model, hopefully it can share what it has learned across tasks and combine skills in ways that we didn’t explicitly train. But that’s also the challenge. Putting everything into one network doesn’t automatically make it more capable. We need to preserve the individual skills while getting useful transfer between them. That’s what would make it a more general robot controller.

r001.rationale: The response hopes the model will share learning and combine skills in untrained ways, but it does not identify interpolation between skills.
